Inequality in England: life expectancy and causes of death by deprivation

Source: vignettes/inequality-england.Rmd
inequality-england.Rmd

This vignette is precomputed (dev/precompute-vignettes.R) because its backtests take several minutes.

How large will the gap in life expectancy between the least and the most deprived areas of England be in 2035, and which causes of death will make it up? A forecast of a gap is more than two forecasts: it depends on how the forecasts of the groups move relative to each other. This vignette builds a pipeline in which every step is chosen in a backtest of the quantity the question is about, the gap. Each step refers to the vignette that explains it.

library(mortensor)
library(data.table)

Data

Deaths and mid-year populations by sex, 5-year age group and decile of the Index of Multiple Deprivation, England 2001-2019 (ons_data; Source: Office for National Statistics, Open Government Licence v3.0), combined into quintiles (Q1 most deprived, Q5 least deprived):

x <- mt_data(deaths = ons_data, population = ons_data, by = c("sex", "imd_decile"), age = "age_group",
             value = c(deaths = "all_causes", population = "population"))
x <- mt_as_exposure(x, type = "midyear")
x <- mt_group_levels(x, "imd_decile", function(d) paste0("Q", ceiling(as.numeric(d) / 2)), name = "quintile")
mt_validate(x)
#> <mt_validation> no findings

The hierarchy. The ten series of sex by quintile add up to England and to both sexes. All forecasts below are made for the ten series and summed (reconciled(method = "bottom_up")), so that England is the sum of its quintiles in every path (“Coherent forecasts: totals and their parts”):

h <- mt_hierarchy(sex = "both", quintile = list(total = "England"))
xa <- mt_aggregate_strata(x, h)
bu <- function(model) reconciled(model, h, method = "bottom_up")

The observed gap in life expectancy at birth between Q5 and Q1:

gap_obs <- mt_contrast(xa, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1")
mt_plot_contrast(observed = gap_obs, levels = "Q5")

For women the gap widened from about 5.2 years in 2001 to 6.5 years in 2019, most of it after 2011. For men it stayed at about 7.5 years, with a dip around 2010.

Part 1: the gap in life expectancy

What the models assume about the gap

The candidates differ in how the quintiles may move relative to each other (“Choosing and combining models”):

  • Lee-Carter and the functional demographic model (fdm), fitted to each quintile separately: each quintile continues its own trend, so a gap that widened keeps widening;
  • Li-Lee and the coherent fdm (product-ratio method): the quintiles of each sex share a common trend, and their deviations from it are stationary, so gaps return towards their past level;
  • an ensemble of Lee-Carter and fdm.

The gap between Q5 and Q1 forecast by three of them:

cand <- list("Lee-Carter" = bu(lee_carter()), "fdm" = bu(hyndman_ullah()),
             "Li-Lee" = bu(li_lee(common_by = "sex")), "coherent fdm" = bu(coherent_fdm(common_by = "sex")),
             "Lee-Carter + fdm" = bu(ensemble(lc = lee_carter(), fdm = hyndman_ullah())))
gaps <- lapply(cand[c("Lee-Carter", "Li-Lee", "coherent fdm")], function(m) {
  mt_contrast(mt_forecast(mt_fit(m, xa), to = 2035, n_draws = 500, seed = 1), var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", at = 0)
})
mt_plot_contrast(gaps, observed = gap_obs, levels = "Q5")

The assumption decides the answer: Lee-Carter continues the widening of the female gap. The two coherent models start below the observed gap of 2019, because their fitted rates of the last year already pull the quintiles towards the common trend, and narrow it further.

Which model forecast the gap best

A backtest from the origins 2010-2014, five years ahead each, scores the rates and life expectancy of every series, and the gap between each quintile and Q1 path by path (contrast, “Backtesting and scores”):

bt <- mt_compare(cand, xa, origins = 2010:2014, h = 5, n_draws = 200, quantities = "life_expectancy",
                 contrast = c(var = "quintile", ref = "Q1"))
mt_score_table(bt, metrics = c("crps", "cov95"), targets = c("rate", "life_expectancy"), hierarchy = h)
#>                model     level   crps cov95 crps_le cov95_le
#>  1:       Lee-Carter    bottom 0.0665 0.834   0.329    0.808
#>  2:       Lee-Carter aggregate 0.0550 0.718   0.349    0.600
#>  3:       Lee-Carter     total 0.0454 0.530   0.368    0.320
#>  4:              fdm    bottom 0.0726 0.828   0.361    0.744
#>  5:              fdm aggregate 0.0594 0.712   0.333    0.594
#>  6:              fdm     total 0.0486 0.524   0.317    0.400
#>  7:           Li-Lee    bottom 0.0671 0.842   0.388    0.756
#>  8:           Li-Lee aggregate 0.0556 0.766   0.389    0.703
#>  9:           Li-Lee     total 0.0474 0.674   0.374    0.720
#> 10:     coherent fdm    bottom 0.0707 0.763   0.413    0.540
#> 11:     coherent fdm aggregate 0.0606 0.657   0.402    0.434
#> 12:     coherent fdm     total 0.0546 0.496   0.381    0.360
#> 13: Lee-Carter + fdm    bottom 0.0657 0.878   0.321    0.864
#> 14: Lee-Carter + fdm aggregate 0.0535 0.782   0.321    0.691
#> 15: Lee-Carter + fdm     total 0.0432 0.566   0.327    0.360
mt_score_table(bt[quintile == "Q5" & sex != "both"], metrics = c("crps", "cov95"), targets = "life_expectancy_gap")
#>               model crps_le_gap cov95_le_gap
#> 1:       Lee-Carter       0.201         0.98
#> 2:              fdm       0.380         0.70
#> 3:           Li-Lee       0.753         0.14
#> 4:     coherent fdm       0.668         0.18
#> 5: Lee-Carter + fdm       0.271         0.96
mt_plot_scores(bt[quintile == "Q5" & sex != "both"], by = "model", target = "life_expectancy_gap")

The models forecast the rates of the quintiles within about 10% of each other, the ensemble best. The intervals of life expectancy are too narrow for every model, most for the totals (95% coverage of Lee-Carter 0.81 for the quintiles and 0.32 for England): five years ahead, the forecasts underestimate how far life expectancy can move. The gap separates the models clearly: Li-Lee and the coherent fdm forecast it worst, and their intervals covered the observed gap in only 14% and 18% of the cases, because in 2010-2019 the female gap did not return to its past level. Lee-Carter forecast the gap best, with intervals that covered it in 98% of the cases, the ensemble of Lee-Carter and fdm second. The pipeline continues with Lee-Carter, chosen for the quantity of the question.

Smoothing and jump-off

Two further choices, each checked in the same backtest: smoothing the rates over time before fitting (“Smoothing death rates”), and starting the forecasts at the observed level of the last three years (“Where a forecast starts: the jump-off”):

steps <- list("Lee-Carter" = cand[["Lee-Carter"]],
              "+ smoothed over time" = list(spec = cand[["Lee-Carter"]], prep = mt_prep(step_smooth(along = "period"))),
              "+ anchored" = bu(anchored(lee_carter(), years = 3)))
bt_steps <- mt_compare(steps, xa, origins = 2010:2014, h = 5, n_draws = 200, quantities = "life_expectancy",
                       contrast = c(var = "quintile", ref = "Q1"))
mt_score_table(bt_steps[sex != "both" & quintile != "England"], metrics = c("crps", "cov95"))
#>                   model   crps cov95 crps_le cov95_le crps_le_gap cov95_le_gap
#> 1:           Lee-Carter 0.0665 0.834   0.329    0.808       0.193        0.985
#> 2: + smoothed over time 0.0753 0.640   0.507    0.200       0.203        0.565
#> 3:           + anchored 0.0665 0.836   0.328    0.788       0.192        0.985

Smoothing over time made the forecasts of the rates and of life expectancy much worse (95% coverage of the rates 0.64 against 0.83, of life expectancy 0.20 against 0.81): the year-to-year variation of these rates is information about the uncertainty, and removing it made the intervals too narrow. The gaps were forecast slightly worse as well, with too narrow intervals (95% coverage 0.57 against 0.98). Anchoring changed almost nothing, because the fitted rates of Lee-Carter in the last year are close to the observed ones. The pipeline uses neither.

Forecast to 2035 

fc <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(cand[["Lee-Carter"]], xa), to = 2035, n_draws = 1000, seed = 1)
mt_plot_life_expectancy(fc, at = 0, facet = "sex", strata = mt_strata(x)$label)

The gap between Q5 and Q1, path by path, and the slope index of inequality (SII: the difference in life expectancy between the bottom and the top of the deprivation distribution, estimated from all five quintiles and their population shares):

gap <- mt_contrast(fc, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", at = 0)
mt_plot_contrast(gap, observed = gap_obs, levels = "Q5")

sii <- mt_inequality(fc, "quintile", order = paste0("Q", 1:5), quantity = "life_expectancy")[index == "sii"]
sii_obs <- mt_inequality(x, "quintile", order = paste0("Q", 1:5), quantity = "life_expectancy")[index == "sii"]
rbind(sii_obs[period == 2019], sii[period %in% c(2025, 2035)])[
  , .(sex, period, sii = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f-%.1f)", q0.5, q0.025, q0.975))]
#>       sex period            sii
#> 1: female   2019  7.7 (7.5-7.9)
#> 2:   male   2019  9.2 (9.1-9.4)
#> 3: female   2025  8.2 (6.7-9.9)
#> 4: female   2035 8.9 (6.5-12.1)
#> 5:   male   2025 9.3 (8.1-11.0)
#> 6:   male   2035 9.3 (7.3-12.4)
#> 7:   both   2025 8.8 (7.8-10.4)
#> 8:   both   2035 9.2 (7.5-12.1)

The SII of women rises from 7.7 years in 2019 to 8.9 years in 2035 (95% interval 6.5-12.1); that of men stays at about 9.3 years.

Which ages make up the gap

The gap between Q5 and Q1 by age, in 2019 and 2035 (“Decomposing differences in life expectancy”):

dg <- mt_decompose(fc, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", periods = c(2019, 2035))
mt_plot_decomposition(dg, by = "age", comparisons = list(to = "Q5", sex = "female"))

In 2019 most of the female gap arose at ages 55-84; by 2035 the contributions move to older ages, with wide intervals.

Part 2: causes of death at ages 50 and over

Data

ons_cause_groups combines the 29 causes of the ONS table into groups with enough deaths in almost every cell at ages 50 and over. The causes share the population of their stratum, so their rates add up to the all-cause rate (additive = "rates"):

causes <- names(ons_data)[-(1:7)]
xc <- mt_data(deaths = ons_data, population = ons_data, by = c("sex", "imd_decile", "cause"),
              age = "age_group", value = list(deaths = c(all = "all_causes", causes), population = "population"))
xc <- mt_as_exposure(xc, type = "midyear")
xc <- mt_subset(xc, ages = c(50, Inf))
xc <- mt_group_levels(xc, "imd_decile", function(d) paste0("Q", ceiling(as.numeric(d) / 2)), name = "quintile")
xc <- mt_group_levels(xc, "cause", ons_cause_groups, other = "rest", total = "all", additive = "rates")
hc <- mt_hierarchy(cause = "all", additive = "rates")
mt_validate(xc, hierarchy = hc)
#> <mt_validation> 1 finding(s): 0 error, 0 warning, 1 info
#>   [info] hierarchy (deaths,exposure, 10 aggregate strata, n = 0): sums of parts agree with the totals within tolerance

Model: causes that add up to all causes

Cause-specific counts per quintile are small, so the causes are forecast with Li-Lee, the quintiles of each sex and cause pooled around a common trend. Summed over the causes, such forecasts tend to be more pessimistic than forecasts of all causes, because over many years the sum is dominated by the causes that fall slowest or rise (Wilmoth 1995). The alternative is to forecast all causes as well and scale the causes to it, path by path, in proportion to their own forecasts (method = "proportional" with the all-cause strata fixed). Part 1 showed that the all-cause gap is forecast best by Lee-Carter, so stratified() uses Lee-Carter for the all-cause strata and Li-Lee for the causes. Three candidates:

all_cause <- mt_strata(xc)[cause == "all", label]
ll <- li_lee(common_by = c("sex", "cause"))
cand_c <- list("summed" = reconciled(ll, hc, method = "bottom_up"),
               "scaled to Li-Lee total" = reconciled(ll, hc, method = "proportional", fixed = all_cause),
               "scaled to Lee-Carter total" = reconciled(stratified("cause", all = lee_carter(), .default = ll), hc,
                                                         method = "proportional", fixed = all_cause))
bt_c <- mt_compare(cand_c, xc, origins = c(2010, 2012, 2014), h = 5, n_draws = 200,
                   quantities = c("life_expectancy", "asr"), contrast = c(var = "quintile", ref = "Q1"))

For the causes: the age-standardised rates (_asr) and their differences between each quintile and Q1 (_asr_gap, log rate ratios):

mt_score_table(bt_c[cause != "all"], metrics = c("crps", "cov95"), targets = c("asr", "asr_gap"))
#>                         model crps_asr cov95_asr crps_asr_gap cov95_asr_gap
#> 1:                     summed   0.0663     0.808       0.0558         0.621
#> 2:     scaled to Li-Lee total   0.0710     0.876       0.0460         0.771
#> 3: scaled to Lee-Carter total   0.0689     0.847       0.0381         0.997

For all causes: life expectancy at 50 (_le) and its gap to Q1 (_le_gap):

mt_score_table(bt_c[cause == "all"], metrics = c("crps", "cov95"), targets = c("life_expectancy", "life_expectancy_gap"))
#>                         model crps_le cov95_le crps_le_gap cov95_le_gap
#> 1:                     summed   0.277    0.740       0.494        0.125
#> 2:     scaled to Li-Lee total   0.327    0.787       0.329        0.450
#> 3: scaled to Lee-Carter total   0.289    0.740       0.127        0.992

For the causes the three are close: the summed forecasts are slightly the most accurate for the age-standardised rates but the least accurate for their gaps, and those scaled to Lee-Carter forecast the gaps best (95% coverage 0.997). The intervals of the age-standardised rates are too narrow for all three (95% coverage 0.81-0.88). For all causes the difference is large: the summed causes and the Li-Lee total both pull the gap back to its past level, and only the Lee-Carter total forecast it well (CRPS of the gap 0.13 against 0.33 and 0.49).

Forecasts to 2035 

fc_c <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(cand_c[["scaled to Lee-Carter total"]], xc), to = 2035, n_draws = 1000, seed = 1)
#> Warning in check_draws_plausible(arr, fit$age, fit$strata, fit$spec$label): By
#> cause (all: Lee-Carter; other: Li-Lee (common by sex, cause)): forecast death
#> rates above 1 in 0.6% of the draws (strata female.Q1.dementia,
#> female.Q2.dementia, female.Q3.dementia; ages 90+). The model is unstable here,
#> often because of sparse counts or a steep trend extrapolated far ahead;
#> consider wider age groups (mt_regroup()), pooling (li_lee(common_by = )),
#> smoothing (step_smooth()) or an ensemble.
mt_compare_forecasts(list(observed = mt_subset(xc, cause == "all"), forecast = fc_c), periods = c(2019, 2035),
                     strata = c("female.Q1.all", "female.Q5.all", "male.Q1.all", "male.Q5.all"))
#>            label period         observed         forecast
#> 1: female.Q1.all   2019 31.7 (31.6-31.8)             <NA>
#> 2: female.Q1.all   2035             <NA> 33.0 (30.1-35.6)
#> 3: female.Q5.all   2019 37.3 (37.2-37.3)             <NA>
#> 4: female.Q5.all   2035             <NA> 39.9 (37.6-42.2)
#> 5:   male.Q1.all   2019 28.3 (28.3-28.4)             <NA>
#> 6:   male.Q1.all   2035             <NA> 30.8 (29.1-32.5)
#> 7:   male.Q5.all   2019 34.5 (34.4-34.6)             <NA>
#> 8:   male.Q5.all   2035             <NA> 37.4 (36.0-38.7)

The warning concerns dementia at ages 90 and over, whose recorded rates rose steeply in 2001-2019 (partly through changes in coding): a few paths extrapolate this rise to rates above one.

Life expectancy at 50 from all causes, observed in 2019 and forecast for 2035. The ratio of the age-standardised death rates (ages 50 and over) of Q1 to Q5 in 2035, path by path:

ratio <- mt_contrast(fc_c, var = "quintile", ref = "Q5", quantity = "asr", type = "ratio")
ratio[level == "Q1" & period == 2035 & cause != "all",
      .(sex, cause, ratio = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f-%.2f)", q0.5, q0.025, q0.975))][order(sex, cause)]
#>        sex             cause            ratio
#>  1: female   breast_prostate 1.42 (1.05-2.03)
#>  2: female colorectal_cancer 1.56 (1.01-2.41)
#>  3: female          dementia 1.69 (0.72-3.19)
#>  4: female          diabetes 2.82 (1.25-6.61)
#>  5: female               ihd 2.79 (1.73-4.78)
#>  6: female     liver_alcohol 3.60 (1.99-5.94)
#>  7: female       lung_cancer 3.56 (2.38-5.37)
#>  8: female     other_cancers 1.78 (1.26-2.91)
#>  9: female other_circulatory 2.04 (0.60-5.47)
#> 10: female       respiratory 4.29 (2.63-6.84)
#> 11: female              rest 1.92 (1.10-5.06)
#> 12: female            stroke 1.82 (1.01-3.20)
#> 13:   male   breast_prostate 1.15 (0.75-2.10)
#> 14:   male colorectal_cancer 1.57 (1.09-2.40)
#> 15:   male          dementia 1.68 (0.46-4.10)
#> 16:   male          diabetes 2.60 (0.81-6.73)
#> 17:   male               ihd 2.24 (1.42-3.63)
#> 18:   male     liver_alcohol 4.20 (2.87-5.67)
#> 19:   male       lung_cancer 3.03 (2.27-4.30)
#> 20:   male     other_cancers 1.68 (1.05-2.41)
#> 21:   male other_circulatory 1.86 (0.69-3.73)
#> 22:   male       respiratory 3.46 (1.79-7.47)
#> 23:   male              rest 1.83 (1.12-2.99)
#> 24:   male            stroke 1.82 (1.01-3.84)
#>        sex             cause            ratio
mt_plot_shares(fc_c, groups = c("female.Q1", "female.Q5", "male.Q1", "male.Q5"))

Proportional scaling has a consequence for these ratios: where the all-cause gap widens, the widening is spread over all causes in proportion to their forecasts, so the ratios of every cause rise somewhat. Which causes will in fact drive a widening is not in the data.

Which causes make up the gap

The gap in life expectancy at 50 between Q5 and Q1 by cause, observed in 2019 and forecast for 2035:

dc <- mt_decompose(fc_c, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", periods = c(2019, 2035), cause = "cause")
mt_plot_decomposition(dc, by = "cause", comparisons = list(to = "Q5", sex = "female"))

In 2019 the residual group, chronic lower respiratory diseases, lung cancer and ischaemic heart disease made up most of the female gap at 50. The forecast for 2035 gives dementia the largest contribution, but with an interval from below zero to about three years: it extrapolates the steep rise of recorded dementia deaths, which partly reflects changes in coding. This is the least reliable part of the result.

Summary of the pipeline

Step Decision here Evidence Function Explained in
Data deciles to quintiles mt_data(), mt_group_levels() “Getting started”
Totals England and both sexes as sums mt_hierarchy(), reconciled(method = "bottom_up") “Coherent forecasts”
Model Lee-Carter per quintile best backtest of the gap mt_compare(contrast = ) “Choosing and combining models”
Smoothing none made every score worse step_smooth() “Smoothing death rates”
Jump-off the model’s own anchoring changed nothing anchored() “Where a forecast starts”
Inequality gap Q5 - Q1 and SII, path by path mt_contrast(), mt_inequality()
Causes Li-Lee, scaled to a Lee-Carter all-cause forecast best backtest of the all-cause gap stratified(), reconciled(method = "proportional", fixed = ) “Coherent forecasts”
Drivers ages and causes of the gap mt_decompose() “Decomposing differences”

References

Wilmoth JR (1995). Are mortality projections always more pessimistic when disaggregated by cause of death? Mathematical Population Studies 5(4): 293-319. doi:10.1080/08898489509525409.
